title: Git, tooling, CI/CD and deployment
blurb: Branching, undoing mistakes, what the pipeline does, containers and environments. Everyone claims to know Git — this is where that gets tested.

questions.q: What is the difference between merge and rebase?
choices: Merge creates a commit joining two histories; rebase replays your commits on top of another branch, rewriting them
questions.why: Rebase gives linear, readable history. Because it rewrites commits, never rebase a branch other people have pulled — their history and yours diverge and the next merge is a mess.
questions.asked: Guaranteed. The 'never rebase shared branches' caveat is the part that matters.

questions.q: You committed to `main` instead of a feature branch, and have not pushed. What now?
choices: Create the branch at the current commit, then reset main back to origin/main
questions.why: `git branch feature`, then `git reset --hard origin/main` while on main. The commit is safe on the new branch. Nothing was pushed, so nobody else is affected.
questions.asked: A practical scenario question — the answer shows whether you actually understand branches as pointers.

questions.q: What is the difference between `git revert` and `git reset`?
choices: revert adds a new commit undoing a change (safe on shared branches); reset moves the branch pointer, rewriting history
revert deletes the commit, reset keeps it
They are the same for pushed commits
reset is for files, revert for commits
questions.why: If it is already pushed, revert. Reset on a shared branch means everyone else's history disagrees with the remote and someone will force-push over someone's work.

questions.q: What does `git reset --soft`, `--mixed` and `--hard` each keep?
choices: soft keeps staged changes, mixed keeps them unstaged, hard discards them entirely
soft is for files, hard for branches
hard is the only one that moves HEAD
questions.why: `--hard` is the only Git command that routinely destroys uncommitted work — and it is the one people run when panicking. Commit or stash first.

questions.q: What is `git stash` for?
choices: Temporarily shelving uncommitted changes so you can switch context, then reapply them
questions.why: Useful, but stashes are easy to forget and do not survive a fresh clone. A throwaway WIP commit on a branch is often the safer habit.

questions.q: What does a `.gitignore` NOT do?
choices: It does not untrack a file that has already been committed
It does not affect new files
It does not work on directories
It does not apply to subfolders
questions.why: You need `git rm --cached`. And if a secret was committed, ignoring it now does nothing — it is still in history, so rotate the credential.

questions.q: What makes a good commit message?
choices: A short imperative summary of what changed, and a body explaining why when it is not obvious
A list of every file touched
As much detail as possible about how
questions.why: The diff already says how. Six months later, `git log` is the only record of why — 'fix bug' tells the next person nothing when they are bisecting a regression.

questions.q: What is `git bisect` for?
choices: Binary searching history to find the commit that introduced a bug
questions.why: Mark a good commit and a bad one and Git walks you through the halves. It is why small, atomic commits pay off — a bisect that lands on a 2000-line commit tells you very little.

questions.q: What should a CI pipeline run before a merge?
choices: Build, lint, type-check, unit and integration tests — everything that must be true for the branch to be mergeable
Only the unit tests, for speed
questions.why: The point is that main is always releasable. Anything you would be embarrassed to merge belongs in the pipeline, and anything not in the pipeline will eventually be skipped.

questions.q: What is the difference between continuous integration and continuous deployment?
choices: CI merges and verifies changes frequently; CD automatically releases every passing build
CD means deploying manually but often
questions.why: Continuous *delivery* means every build is releasable; continuous *deployment* means it actually ships without a human. Plenty of good teams do the former and gate the latter.

questions.q: What is a container, precisely?
choices: An isolated process sharing the host kernel, with its own filesystem and namespaces — not a virtual machine
A lightweight virtual machine with its own kernel
A packaged zip of the application
questions.why: Sharing the kernel is why containers start in milliseconds and VMs take seconds. It is also why a Linux container cannot run on a Windows kernel without a VM underneath.
questions.asked: The 'it's not a VM' distinction is the whole question.

questions.q: What is the point of a multi-stage Dockerfile?
choices: Build with the full SDK, then copy only the artefacts into a small runtime image
To run multiple processes in one container
questions.why: A .NET SDK image is roughly 800MB; the runtime image is a fraction of that. Smaller images pull faster, cost less to store, and contain fewer things a scanner can flag.

questions.q: Why order Dockerfile instructions so dependency installs come before copying source?
choices: Layer caching — a source change should not invalidate the dependency install layer
It reduces the final image size
questions.why: Copy package.json and run install, then copy the rest. Get it backwards and every one-line change reinstalls every dependency, turning a 10-second build into three minutes.

questions.q: How should configuration differ between dev, staging and production?
choices: Same build artefact everywhere, configured by environment variables injected at deploy
questions.why: Build once, promote the same artefact. If you rebuild per environment, the thing you tested is not the thing you shipped.

questions.q: What is a blue/green deployment?
choices: Run the new version alongside the old, switch traffic over, and switch back instantly if it fails
Deploying half the features at a time
questions.why: Rollback is a traffic switch, not a redeploy. The catch is shared state: database schema must work with both versions during the overlap, which is why expand/contract migrations matter.

questions.q: What is a feature flag for?
choices: Separating deploy from release, so code can ship dark and be turned on independently
questions.why: It enables trunk-based development — merge small changes often without half-finished features reaching users. The cost is flag debt; every flag needs a removal date.

questions.q: The pipeline is green but production is broken. What class of problem is this?
choices: Something that only exists in the target environment — config, secrets, data, network, or scale
questions.why: The pipeline validates the artefact, not the environment. This is why smoke tests after deploy and good observability matter more than adding another unit test.
questions.asked: A realistic scenario question. It tests whether you understand the limits of CI.

questions.q: What does semantic versioning promise?
choices: MAJOR breaks compatibility, MINOR adds compatibly, PATCH fixes compatibly
Nothing — it is only a convention for libraries
questions.why: It is a social contract, not an enforced rule, which is why lockfiles exist. For an application (rather than a library) it often matters less than a traceable build number.

questions.q: What is trunk-based development?
choices: Short-lived branches merged to main frequently, keeping main always releasable
Committing directly to main with no review
questions.why: The alternative — long-lived branches — produces enormous merges and integration pain. The trade-off is that incomplete work must be hidden behind flags.

questions.q: Someone force-pushed over your commits on a shared branch. Are they gone?
choices: Usually recoverable — `git reflog` locally, or the old commit SHA on the remote, still points at them
Only if you had pushed them
questions.why: Git rarely deletes objects immediately; the reflog records where HEAD has been. The real lesson is to protect main and require pull requests so this cannot happen.

questions.q: What is the difference between `npm install` and `npm ci`?
choices: install may update the lockfile; ci installs strictly from it and fails if package.json disagrees
install works offline, ci does not
questions.why: `npm ci` wipes node_modules and reproduces the lockfile exactly — which is what you want in a pipeline, where a surprise dependency upgrade should be an error, not a silent event.

questions.q: What does a linter give you that the compiler does not?
choices: Rules about style and likely-wrong-but-legal code, enforced consistently without review debate
questions.why: `no-floating-promises` and the React hooks rules catch real bugs a type checker will not. Automating style also removes the least valuable category of review comment.

questions.q: Why should build artefacts and `node_modules` not be in version control?
choices: They are derived, huge, platform-specific and generate constant conflicts
questions.why: Commit the lockfile — the recipe — not the result. Native modules compiled on your machine will not even run on the build server.

questions.q: What is a rolling deployment's main constraint?
choices: Old and new versions run simultaneously, so both must work against the same database and API contracts
questions.why: This is why you never rename a column and deploy the code in the same release. Add, backfill, dual-write, migrate reads, then remove — across several deploys.
questions.asked: It connects deployment strategy to database migrations, which is a genuinely mid-level connection to make.
